speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house of a change in the ministry, in that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra was sworn in this morning before His Excellency the Governor General as Secretary of State for External Affairs.

maintopic: THE MINISTRY
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: THE MINISTRY
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that seldom when I rise does there seem to be this degree of unanimity in the response. I must express my own thanks for the manner in which the house has received the announcement.
I might add something more. I know hon. members in the opposition particularly would not want to be denied the opportunity of questioning the new minister when the public works estimates are before the committee, and until the conclusion of those estimates he will also continue to discharge his responsibilities as Minister of Public Works. I think I should add as well that until the end of this session, in any event, he will remain in his position as house leader.
I say no more than that. I simply wanted to place before the house this change. I merely add in the simplest words, and I know I speak for the members of this house and the people of Canada as a whole, my hope that in the discharge of this new field of responsibilities his achievements of the past will be maintained in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of fhe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE MINISTRY
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first reaction on hearing this news is the feeling that in due course, because of the heavy responsibilities of his new post as Secretary of State for External Affairs, as well as Minister of Public Works, he will probably have to give up the house leadership.
I want to assure him that if and when that happens we shall miss his kindly advice and his engaging admonitions. He will no doubt reserve them for international assemblies in the future.
We on this side of the house wish him well in a post which, I know from some
experience, is as exacting as it is rewarding. There can, I think, be no greater privilege and perhaps no greater responsibility for a Canadian than that of speaking for his country in the councils of the world and to have what I might call a primary responsibility, under the Prime Minister, for shaping foreign policies at a time when everything we hope for-our destiny, our very existence-depends on the success of those policies in maintaining peace and strengthening security.
The minister, who has the regard, the esteem and perhaps I can say the affection of every member of this house, can be assured of our good will and our good wishes in his new work. He can also, I think, expect to receive-and I am speaking now for the official opposition-our support in every strong and forward-looking Canadian move that he may initiate to keep our country's position high and respected in the world and in pursuing the objectives that we all share, whatever the party to which we may belong, namely good relations among all peoples in a world of peace and freedom.

maintopic: THE MINISTRY
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group and on behalf of the people of British Columbia, as the hon. member for Kootenay West and as the honorary president of the 54th Kootenay battalion association, and as a former comrade in arms-something of which I am always proud-I extend sincere and warm congratulations to the minister on his appointment as Secretary of State for External Affairs.
While all members of this house wish him well and every success with his new responsibilities, the people of Kootenay West, regardless of party, will derive a particular satisfaction and pleasure from his appointment to this high office. The residents of his home town of Kaslo, where he was born, will be proud of this further distinction bestowed on a native son. His old comrades in the 54th Kootenay battalion will rejoice in his opportunity to serve in the front line of international affairs.
Mr. Speaker, the minister faces heavy responsibilities and tremendous issues and problems-and he has our good will in that respect-which include consideration of the abandonment of nuclear tests; proposals for progressive disarmament as the result of negotiation and agreement; the churning problems of the Middle East and the Far East. Those problems will tax his patience and

Ministerial Appointment his ability to the limit. In facing those problems the C.C.F. believe that Canada can best play a positive role and exercise a positive influence for peace by pursuing an independent but co-operative policy in international affairs.
This appointment provides the minister with an opportunity to paint some large brush strokes on the canvas of Canadian history to complement the many finer lines he has drawn during his long service as a member of this house and a member of this government. We sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that from this appointment, this opportunity and the essence of the minister's recognized ability and trustworthiness will be distilled solid achievements toward the building of world peace.

maintopic: THE MINISTRY
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was intended to be serious. As for the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), I am very touched by his remarks. As he has said, we were comrades in the 54th Kootenay battalion in the first war. About 44 years ago we enlisted in the city of Nelson in the same company, and from those days on there has been a great friendship between us. When he spoke today I think he spoke with a little bias in my favour. However, I shall pay great heed to the sage words he has uttered this afternoon.
I am also very grateful for the response given by the other members of this House of Commons. Sometimes I think we do not fully appreciate the great strength, for our nation, of parliament. It has become a commonplace in a way, and we do not always realize how vitally important it is in the life of a democratic nation. Last night I was thinking of some of the days in parliament since I have been here. About 19 years ago there was a terribly black day when France was falling and Hon. Norman Rogers was killed in an aeroplane crash. Because of that crash Canada lost one of her most promising public men. Everything was black; I have never known such a black day in my life. Yet there was no one in this house or in the Senate who spoke of surrender or defeat. The sitting was postponed for an hour because of the tragedy of Norman Rogers' death, but on that occasion, as on so many other occasions during the war, this house faced the terrible problems of the time and, I think, was a splendid example of what parliament should be.
I should like hon. members to feel that in this new post I shall always look to the house for help and guidance. After all, we have here a gathering of the representatives of Canadians from coast to coast, a great body of representatives who come to this assembly, and moving together I believe we can solve any problem which faces the nation. In these words I should like to include the members of the Senate-I know Your Honour will overlook it if I do not refer to them as members of the other place. They too have made a splendid contribution, and their old friends in the commons have often taken this little walk down to the other end of the building to visit them. In that body there is a wealth of experience and a wealth of common sense. I know that any secretary of state for external affairs will receive help from the members of the Canadian Senate.
It is rather thrilling to be in a position to represent one's nation, . particularly when

that nation happens to be Canada. Those hon. members who served in the first world war will remember the magic of those six letters "Canada" on their shoulder straps, and I am sure there was the same pride in the minds of young Canadians who carried those letters in the second world war. It will be a wonderful thing to be in a position to speak for Canada; but as the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Kootenay West pointed out, in these days it is not sufficient to have great pride in one's nation. We all realize that world events have moved so far in recent years that now the main thing is co-operation among all the nations of the world.
In this new post it will be my endeavour to keep that in mind at all times and to do my part to see to it that Canada maintains the high position in which she has been placed by my predecessors in this office.
I would not like to close without a word about my predecessor, Hon. Sidney Smith. Only those of us who sat with him in cabinet meetings could fully appreciate the sterling character of the man, a great individual. He came here from the presidency of the largest university in Canada with a record of achievement in the university field which I do not think has been excelled at any time in our country, and took on this portfolio. I am convinced that he accepted the portfolio in the belief that he should at least do his part to further the cause of peace in the world. While he was not privileged to carry on for a great length of time I know we will all agree that he did maintain the traditions of that post, that he set a very high standard, and that his service here was not in vain. In the days ahead I shall be trying to keep on the trail which has been blazed by Hon. Sidney Smith. I thank the hon. members very much.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish now to reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie River and in conjunction with the reply to make an announcement. The hon. gentleman asked me a question with regard to a statement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in an article respecting, as it is stated in the article-
-the federal government's decision that a railway connection is to be extended to the south shore of Great Slave lake.
I would point out that in so far as that announcement was concerned there was nothing 66968-9-274
Transport
unusual in it, in that it had been specifically dealt with in the speech from the throne in 1958. With the leave of the house I should like to refer to one sentence in that speech from the throne preparatory to the statement I wish to make. The speech from the throne is recorded at page 5 of Hansard of May 12, 1958. These words were included in those uttered by His Excellency the Governor General:
In order to promote our national development on the frontier in the north you will be asked to authorize the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. My ministers regard this as a major step in the establishment of productive industry on an economic basis in the Northwest Territories.
Since that date the fullest consideration has been given to this question and a number of suggestions have been made as to alternative routes. There have been two major suggestions and I understand eight other alternatives. The proponents of each of these several projected routes have advanced their arguments in support of the particular venture or project which they have in mind.
With a view to hearing the representations that have been and can be made, and reviewing them, the governor in council has set up an inquiry under part I of the Inquiries Act to deal with the alternative routes for a railway line from northern Alberta to Great Slave lake. I ask leave to table copies of the order in council, the material section of which sets out the powers in question:
-to inquire into and report upon the respective merits of the alternative routes which might be followed by a railway line to be built from northern Alberta into the southern portion of the district of Mackenzie, Northwest Territories, for the purpose of providing access to and contributing to the development of that portion of the territories tributary to Great Slave lake.
The commission in question will consist of three men, Mr. Marshall Manning, Q.C., of Edmonton, Mr. W. D. Gainer, an agricultural economist from the University of Alberta in Edmonton, and Mr. John Anderson-Thompson of Yellowknife, Mr. Manning being the chairman of the inquiry. I hope this group will be able to start a full inquiry very shortly, and will be able to report at as early a date as is convenient and possible.

subtopic: GREAT SLAVE LAKE-COMMISSION TO INQUIRE INTO ROUTE OF PROPOSED RAILWAY

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that upon hearing this announcement the people of the Mackenzie River district will be very sad indeed, when they consider that during the last election campaign there was no talk of which route would be followed. The route was chosen. I am sure this is another means of stalling the building of the railway, and I am certain that the people of Mackenzie district will look upon it in that way.

Mr. Speaker, while not announcing the appointment as of this date I wish to advise that the government has decided to appoint as chairman of the civil service commission Hon. Samuel Harvey Shirecliffe Hughes, now a justice of the high court of justice in the province of Ontario, the appointment to become effective on the termination of the present legal term on June 30. At that time his resignation will become effective and the appointment as chairman will begin on the next day.
Mr. Justice Hughes received his early education at Stoke Clark preparatory school, Guildford, England, and Stowe school, Buckingham, England. In Canada he attended Upper Canada College and the University of Toronto. He then attended Oxford, receiving his master of arts degree and became a Queen's counsel in 1955. In the same year, following a successful law practice, he was appointed chairman of the Ontario highway transport board, a position he held until his appointment as a justice in June of 1958. Mr. Justice Hughes, as I said a moment ago, will continue his services as a justice to the end of the term, when his resignation will become effective, and he will then be in a position to take over this high and responsible post.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the new and distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs arising out of a newspaper report in the Montreal Star of May 30, in which it is stated that permission has been granted by the United States treasury department for the passage through the St. Lawrence seaway of the Soviet freighter Ivan Moskvin, bound for Sarnia, Ontario, to pick up a cargo of carbon black, and that the Canadian and Soviet embassies have been informed of this decision. Would the minister care to comment on this report? Can he assure the house that the passage through the St. Lawrence seaway of a foreign vessel bound for a Canadian port will not depend upon any decision of the United States government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PASSAGE OF SOVIET FREIGHTER THROUGH ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me written notice of this question. I have seen the report in the Montreal Star to which the question refers, and it is not entirely accurate. My understanding of the situation is that Soviet representatives asked the United States authorities whether a Soviet vessel would be allowed to use the United States locks in the St. Lawrence seaway. In due course they were told that if an application were made to the seaway administration for the use of the United States facilities by this particular vessel, there would be no objection. The hon. member will, I am sure, appreciate that neither Canada nor the United States has treaty obligations with respect to shipping and commercial arrangements with the Soviet union.
It is, of course, correct that United States permission is required for any vessel to pass through United States waters and facilities, just as Canadian permission is required for any vessel to pass through Canadian waters and facilities.
I would prefer, Mr. Speaker, not to comment on this matter further at the present time.

INQUIRY AS TO FRENCH EDITION OF "TRADE AND commerce"
On the orders of the day:

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last Monday, June 1, I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he could give me a reason why Commerce Exterieur is not an exact translation of Trade and Commerce, and why it is published monthly when the other one is published bimonthly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Foreign Trade and its French language counterpart, Commerce Exterieur, is a publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce devoted almost exclusively to the promotion of Canadian export trade. The circulation of Commerce Exterieur has always been small, despite repeated efforts to increase it with the co-operation of the chambres de commerce in the province of Quebec and the Quebec department of trade and commerce. The paid circulation during the fiscal year 1958-59 was 183 subscriptions. On this basis, with printing costs amounting to nearly $10,000, average cost per subscriber was just over $54 per year.
In the light of these circumstances the department came to the conclusion that it was not justified in producing Commerce Exterieur as frequently as the English language counterpart. Therefore in February 1954-and I ask hon. members to note the date-when Foreign Trade was changed from weekly to once every two weeks, the publication of Commerce Exterieur was altered to once a month. Its content differs from that of Foreign Trade only in that certain material of secondary importance is omitted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, June 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-41, to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one can suggest that the subject of dominion-provincial fiscal relations has not received plenty of debate in the course of the present session. On February 9 and 10 the house debated an opposition amendment to a supply motion on this subject. On March 11 I introduced the resolution preceding the present measure. It was debated that day and again on April 30, when the present bill was given first reading. The debate on second reading was continued on May 6, June 2, 3 and 4. The result of this protracted debate over a quite simple and clear measure has been that since March 31 the provinces, which are anxiously waiting to receive the benefit of the present measure, have been deprived of the benefit of the increased payments which it would provide.
It is perhaps not amiss at this point in the debate to recall what is the principle of this measure. It is to provide an increase in the payments out of the federal treasury to the provinces. It is to provide a division of the yield from the standard taxes which will be more generous to the provinces. Notwithstanding our own federal budget problems we believe, and show in this measure that we believe, more generous provision should be made for the provinces than was made under the Liberal regime that preceded us. We said so during the debate on the

Dominion-Provincial Relations Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act in the session of 1956. In proceeding as we are in this present measure we are carrying into statutory fulfilment the statements we made at that time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Will the minister allow a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that I shall be obliged to ask the hon. member to defer his question. I am working under a time limit. There will be a committee stage after this debate is concluded, and I shall be glad to deal with the question then.
When we came into office in 1957 we found nine agreements entered into between the dominion and the provinces in pursuance of this legislation. However unsatisfactory that legislation may have been, however unwillingly many of these provinces entered into those agreements, nevertheless those agreements were a fact and there could be no suggestion of any repudiation thereof. Those agreements in all cases run for the five-year period that the legislation is in effect, to March 31, 1962. That fact, namely the fact of the existence of the nine agreements, is something that must be taken into account by anyone who approaches fairly this present situation in the light of the statements made in the debates in this house in 1956 when the legislation was before the house.
It is a strange scene that we have witnessed in this house, Mr. Speaker, in the course of this debate. Those opposite, who in the days when they were in power were unyielding and unbending in the face of the pleas of the provinces and the municipalities, those same hon. gentlemen who took a highhanded, take it or leave it attitude in dominion-provincial conferences-

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: -now seek somehow to cajole this house and the Canadian people into thinking they have become the champions of the rights of the provinces. Mr. Speaker, it will take a better effort than they have been able to put up in this debate to make that pretence stick. They will need a better disguise than the one they have donned in the course of this debate. The clothes they have attempted to wear in this debate do not fit them at all. AJfter their record they will never be able to appear in this house as champions of the rights of the provinces. They pretend now that more should be done for the provinces. Our answer must be put very simply in the form of a now famous question, Mr. Speaker, and I direct it to them: "Why didn't you do it?"

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: You did not.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
This measure which is before us today would not now be before the house at all if hon. gentlemen opposite had done what they should have done in 1956. How it galls them to be reminded of these simple facts, Mr. Speaker. Their whole attitude in this debate has been one of pretence.
The hon. member for Essex East yesterday made his great plea for the municipalities of this country. I say to that hon. gentleman, when he was a member of the government why did he not do it? Why did not his government do it? And I put these same questions to such hon. members as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who have spoken in this debate about the provinces. The fact that Newfoundland is so much better off today than it was in the days when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and his friends constituted the government obliges one to ask why, in the face of this hypocritical pretence that they have been making in this debate, they did not do something to help out Newfoundland when they were in office.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE

Having regard to our national responsibilities and commitments, we cannot see how we can go further. Under all the circumstances we believe our offer is eminently fair and that it is reasonable and realistic in the light of federal and provincial responsibilities

We cannot at this time make any further material concessions that would adversely affect our revenues.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, these hon. members who now come forward and try to pretend that they are the friends of the provinces and say something more should be done for the provinces are the very members who said, in 1956 when they were in the government, "Not another cent for the provinces". It will be clearly realized that that government, and those hon. members who have been the spokesmen for the opposition in the house during this debate, in those lays banged, barred and bolted the door to the provinces in the face of their pleas for further assistance.

Thus today we ask parliamentary approval to increase the payments to the provinces, and point out that we are doing this at a time when budgetary conditions are much less favourable than they were in 1955 and 1956. The Liberal government of that day had a large surplus then, and its action at that time in refusing to do any more for the provinces can be compared with that of the Conservative government of today which has a deficit, but which is yet prepared to increase that deficit in order to increase payments to the provinces. There is the difference.
We have heard a great deal about unilateral action on the part of the government in this respect. Let us examine that empty assertion. A year ago we asked the house, and the house agreed, to provide this additional 3 per cent to the provinces for a year. We are asking now for an extension of those provisions for another year. We say that the extension will be worth $52 million to those provinces, on the basis of existing estimates. This is excluding the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant and the adjustment to the province of Quebec in terms of its right to collect certain corporation taxes. Or it is worth an estimated $66 million this year if one includes the additional taxes which the province of Quebec is in a position to collect under the terms of the act.
To listen to the speeches made by hon. gentlemen opposite one would think we were imposing some hard bargain on the provinces, inflicting some burden on them. The facts are the very opposite. I wish the hon. members on that side of the house would not depart so far from the facts when they speak on this subject. Here are the facts. The provinces want this additional 3 per cent; they are urgently asking for it; they are unanimous in asking for it. This is the situation, yet all the Liberal members in this house talk about a one-sided deal.

Dominion-Provincial Relations the mistakes which the opposition have been making in this debate, but there is not time. We have rarely seen a debate in which the opposition was so completely befuddled as in this debate on this subject, but let me mention two or three examples. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) was quite confused in what he had to say about these percentages and the relation of these percentages to the taxes collected, and there was an echo of the same misunderstanding in the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier the other evening. He referred to the increase in the federal tax rates and seemed to be under the impression that as a result the provinces were going to receive a smaller share of the yield. The standard corporation tax is, of course, directly related to corporation profits and thus the provincial share is constant, regardless of any change in the level of federal taxation up or down. The individual tax rate is related to the federal level, but is adjusted to the 1956 tax rates, so that there will be no effect on the provincial share from unilateral federal changes.
Thus, in 1958-59 we paid not 13 per cent but at the rate of 14.48 per cent in terms of the yield of that year, and in this year 1959-60 we shall be paying at the rate of 14.18 per cent in terms of the tax yield of this year. This stabilized provincial share was at the request of the provinces which did not wish their proportion of these tax fields to vary with federal tax changes. So, in effect, under this government, it has not been, as was the case under the Liberal government, a formula of 10-9-50; it has not even been a formula of 13-9-50. Last year, it was a formula of 14.48-9-50, and this year it will be 14.18-9-50.
Then we were told by the hon. member for Laurier that the federal government is collecting a larger share of the tax dollar. The fact is that as a result of the larger transfer payments we are making for the benefit of other governments the amount remaining to the federal government is relatively smaller than it was under the Liberal government.

facing both the federal and provincial governments. That is why a much more extensive investigation and study has been called for in order to seek mutually satisfactory solutions. A plenary conference over two or three days can generally solve very little.

The experience of the previous government would indicate that it would likely result in an arbitrary position being assumed. If this federal government were to come to the table as did the previous Liberal government, with its mind all made up, little would be accomplished. Therefore the purpose of these conferences is to prepare the ground for subsequent negotiations although in the process they may be able to resolve some of the detailed technical and procedural problems. The value of this proposed conference is fully recognized by the provinces and the scope of its inquiries will be as unlimited as the provinces may desire.
Let me make it quite clear that as we see it this is the first step in a genuine co-operative effort to develop some mutually satisfactory long term solution. It is not a substitute for a plenary conference of prime minister and premiers but it is a necessary antecedent to the success of any such conference. So I say of the agenda that the agenda is being compiled in consultation with the provinces. We have invited their proposals on the widest scale. This is in no sense going to be an agenda dictated or compiled simply by the federal government. It is going to be an agenda compiled by co-operative effort on the part of the federal and provincial governments.
The meeting of the federal-provincial continuing committee which will follow will undoubtedly result in intensive studies being made not merely by federal officials but, we trust, by officials of all governments, and further exchanges and meetings, if they prove necessary, will be had because this committee will be reporting back to the conference of finance ministers and provincial treasurers and further meetings of the ministers will be invited to be held as may be necessary.

well of the abatement of tax in the province of Quebec on income tax the benefit to the provinces is $66 million under this measure, and that does not include one cent of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant. They are the benefits that this government is seeking to bring to these provinces today and we trust that the house will support us in our effort.
