speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I now ask the minister whether the government will, at the forthcoming July conference, consider favourably the provinces' request or the request of some provinces that this formula should be further modified to a 15-15-50 basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition is asking me to commit myself or to commit the government to some specific increase. Obviously, while the conference will have the widest scope to discuss all questions, I could not possibly be expected to make a statement of the nature asked of me by the Leader of the Opposition at this point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I ask the minister what is the position of the minister with reference to the concrete proposal which was put forward at the November conference of 1957 by the premier of Ontario to the effect that the division should be 15-15-50 rather than the present 13-9-50?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: My position is this. The representatives of any government at this forthcoming conference will be perfectly at liberty to suggest for inclusion in the agenda the discussion of any matter relating to the subject of federal-provincial fiscal relations that commends itself to the conference.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I am sure that is the case, and I am sure that no one on this side of the house or on the other side of it would want to preclude the discussion of any proposal.

But that was not my question. My question to the minister was this. What is the position of the minister with reference to the proposal which was made by the premier of Ontario and supported by several other premiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I have stated my position on that subject.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I proceed a bit further? Am I right in assuming that the position put forward by the premier of Ontario and other premiers was to the effect that the rate should be increased to 15-15-50?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I think that position was taken by the premier of Ontario. As I recall it, I do not think he was the only premier who took that position. I know Premier Roblin of Manitoba has taken it.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Campbell took it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
And others took
it at the conference of November, 1957.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Has the minister given any consideration to the amount which would be required to meet that proposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Yes, from time
to time. But first, Mr. Chairman, we have to make calculations. This is a field in which calculations are being constantly made, because the payments to the provinces undergo change in the light of the yield from period to period from these particular taxes. We have to make an estimate at the beginning of the fiscal year as to what we think the yield is likely to be. That is modified from time to time, and consequently in this field we are making calculations very frequently. It would not be difficult, I suppose, to calculate what the amount would be on any given percentage or any formula, the one mentioned by the hon. gentleman which, I take it, he advocates, or any other formula as applied to a division between the dominion and provincial governments of the yields from these three taxes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Could the minister give the
house the amount of increase in taxation which will be required to bring this payment about and what it would mean in the way of dollars and cents to the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I have not worked this out myself, Mr. Chairman, but I am informed that on a 15-15-50 formula the additional yield to Ontario over and above what will be provided by the present measure would be roughly in the neighbourhood of $100 million. The over-all cost in respect of all provinces-that is, the cost to the federal treasury-would be approximately $275 million.
Dominion-Provincial Relations

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Before I ask the other question, would the minister while I am posing the question be good enough to get the analagous figure for the province of Quebec? The other question which I would like to ask now, and I come back to it again, is what is the-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I am sorry, but
I am not in a position to give what the figure would be for Quebec. That would raise questions as to the tax abatement, and the situation is not as simple to calculate in the case of the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Yes, I realize that. Could I get it at a later date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am afraid I could not obtain it for my hon. friend today but I will be glad to send it to my hon. friend later.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I understand it is in the old
tables and perhaps could be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The figure may have changed from the old tables, depending on the changes in the yields since.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Then I come back to the question again: What is the position of the minister with reference to this proposal, which means in effect an increase to Ontario of $100 million, and I am sure an increase to the province of Quebec of a substantial amount as well, with the other provinces' shares being increased in proportion? Will the hon. minister not tell the house what his attitude or opinion is vis-a-vis that proposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I think this is the third time my hon. friend has asked me the same question. I must refer him to my previous answer.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think notwithstanding what the minister has replied that the committee is entitled to an answer to that question. After all, it has been discussed not only here but elsewhere, and I think the least the minister can do is to tell the house what his attitude or that of the government is with reference to that proposal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
While the minister is thinking or rethinking about that question, may I ask him if the impression which I got from his statement this afternoon about the July conference with the provinces is correct, that it is expected to last for two days only, and that its purpose is to initiate a broad-based examination of federal-provincial fiscal relationships by a joint committee of the provincial governments and the federal government? Is that the purpose of the forthcoming conference?

Dominion-Provincial Relations

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I think the Leader of the Opposition has stated it rather more narrowly than I stated it in my remarks this afternoon, Mr. Chairman. The conference of ministers will open on Monday morning, July 6, at 10.00 o'clock. It will last as long as it is necessary to reach the decisions that the ministers may care to take at that meeting. It is expected in any event that the meeting will go two days. It may go longer, I do not know.
Immediately following that meeting it is expected that the meeting of the continuing committee will follow, and that meeting will proceed as long as may be required. The agenda has not yet been fully determined. There have been confidential communications between the dominion and provincial ministers in regard to it and, as I say, it is now in process of being decided upon between them. I may say that thus far the course of discussion and the response of the provinces indicate that the agenda will be a very wide one and the ministers will be called upon to decide what particular subjects they propose to take up, in what order, what priorities they intend to assign to different subjects, and what subjects they wish the continuing committee of officials, very competent officials indeed, to undertake.
Then at the meeting of the federal-provincial continuing committee the assignment which will come to them from the meeting of ministers will be undertaken and the tasks allotted, as that committee may choose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the representatives of any provincial government at the forthcoming conference should initiate or introduce a proposal for a further modification of this formula to, say, 15-15-50, would that proposal be discussed at this conference and would there be an opportunity afforded of coming to a decision in regard to it at this conference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am quite sure, Mr. Chairman, that there will be discussion of formulae. I cannot imagine this meeting proceeding very far without the question of the formulae being discussed and how formulae can best be made up, having regard to the interest of all parties. Whether any decision can be expected to be taken at that conference I doubt. I do not say decisions cannot be taken. If there were unanimity on some particular subject, I presume the conference, or those who represent the governments at the conference, can obtain instructions; but failing that situation where there is unanimity on such a subject, I presume these subjects would be embraced within the discussions and the studies to follow.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I go one step further and ask the minister if it is accurate to say that at this forthcoming conference there would be an opportunity for a representative of the government of Ontario to advocate a 15-15-50 formula and that there would be at least an opportunity for discussion and decision in regard to that formula?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: As I have stressed, the agenda is a matter for decision on the part of all concerned, and with regard to any answer I may offer with relation to the agenda I wish to make it quite clear that the decision as to what shall be included within the agenda rests with the representatives of all the 11 governments concerned. I have indicated that I would be surprised if there were no discussion about formulas and about matters related to formulas.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Has the attention of the minister been drawn to a statement by the premier of Ontario made in Ottawa on May 29 that he is confident that this federal-provincial parley in Ottawa in July will put a further $100 million or $115 million or $150 million into the revenues of Ontario, and does he feel it is realistic to assume that any decision in this regard could be made in July?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I have not seen the newspaper comment which the hon. member has read.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister
could give an explanation with regard to the figure for British Columbia, which appears to be receiving in extra grants $1,895,000 as compared with a figure of $5 million for Alberta and $24 million for Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The figures I gave at the conclusion of my remarks this afternoon are the estimated figures as of the present time and take into account all the elements including the stabilization payments, and the reason why the figure in the case of British Columbia, which is $1,895,000, is less than the figure of $5,009,000 for the province of Alberta is that British Columbia is a principal beneficiary from the stabilization provisions of this act. The two provinces which have derived most benefit from the stabilization principle are British Columbia and Prince Edward Island, and this lower payment arises because of that principle of a built-in floor from which British Columbia has derived a good deal of protection of its payments hitherto. That is why the increase in this case does not appear to be as much as in the case of its neighbour province.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I wonder whether I may ask the minister this: has the premier of British

Columbia made any representations regarding the bill now before us in connection with another meeting of premiers with the Prime Minister and, if he has, what was the tenor of those representations?
I should also like to ask the minister to tell us as nearly as he is able what was the payment to British Columbia under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act for the year ending March 31, 1958 and also for the year ending March 31, 1959. I should also like the minister to indicate the amount of the estimated payments to British Columbia for the fiscal year which will end on March 31, of next year, 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: There have been to my knowledge no representations received from Premier Bennett in regard to the present amending bill. As to the payments made to British Columbia, I can give the hon. member these figures: for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958 the payments under this act amounted to $58.9 million; in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1959, $64.1 million; in the present fiscal year 1959-60 it is estimated that the payments on the basis of the formula proposed in the present bill will amount to $68.4 million.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I know the minister has stated that the premier of British Columbia has made no particular representations with regard to the bill now before us, but I wonder whether the hon. gentleman will indicate whether or not the premier of British Columbia has made any representations within the past six or eight months expressing his desire for a new meeting with the Prime Minister of Canada along with the premiers of the various provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I am informed that the purport of the letter from the premier of British Columbia in accepting the invitation to participate in the conference on July 6 indicated that he thought this meeting was a good idea as a useful and necessary preliminary to a plenary conference.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I hope the minister realizes that under the benefits of the legislation now before us the estimated payments to British Columbia will amount to $68.4 million. If we add to that all the various other payments being made by the federal government to the treasury of the British Columbian government, especially under the provisions of the national health insurance act it will be seen that contributions by this government to the revenues of the government of British Columbia will exceed one-third of the income of the government of British Columbia. Therefore, any slogan upon which the government of British Columbia may embark in favour of a larger
Dominion-Provincial Relations amount of money from Ottawa will be based on a somewhat weak foundation inasmuch as Ottawa is even now paying in excess of one-third of the income of the government of British Columbia.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I ask the minister if the change in the rate of standard income tax for the purpose of calculating the payment to the provinces is the only change made by the present government since it took office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
There have been a number of changes made in the terms and the amounts of the payments made by the federal to the provincial governments. May
I	mention just a few? There are, of course, the conditional payments-quite a wide range of them. I should be glad to go into them, but I think that would be outside the scope of the present debate and what is properly relevant to this measure. In the second place there are, of course, the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, and in the third place the provision made for tax abatements and the 3 per cent increase.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Do I understand that the substance of the measure is the same and that this is only a question of amounts and rates- it is a question of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
If the hon. member is confining his question to the unconditional payments made in pursuance of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, that is one thing, but to put his question as broadly as he has done takes in a great deal more territory. Unless he restricts it I would have to answer his question by saying that the payments are greatly expanded and there have been many additions and many changes always in favour of the provinces. On the other hand, if he is confining his question to the terms of the present act, the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, last year's amending act added a new section
II	and a new section 12, and the present bill now before the committee would propose to amend section 12 by extending until March 31, 1960, the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether the government proposes to put forward any plan at the forthcoming conference for a further modification of the existing tax-sharing formula or any new proposal for a tax-sharing formula.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are prepared to discuss any suggestions that are made with relation to the formula and will co-operate in any study that is sought or desired by the provinces in relation to
4332	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations that subject. We are certainly not going into this conference laying down any hard and fast proposals.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I was not sugesting that, Mr. Chairman; I do not think it could be inferred from my question that I was suggesting any such procedure as that would be adopted. I am merely asking whether the federal government apart from its expressed willingness to consider any proposal made by provincial delegations is itself going to put forward for discussion and consideration any modification of this tax-sharing formula or a new formula to replace the present one? Has the government any plans for that purpose? Is it to be a matter for consideration at the conference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there are so many hypothetical elements in the hon. gentleman's questions that I do not think I can usefully add to what I have already said to the committee on the subject.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: There is nothing hypothetical about the deduction one must draw from the minister's evasion. The deduction I draw is that the federal government is not going to propose any further modification of the present formula or any new formula because surely if the government on the eve of this conference had such a proposal to make it would at least be able to inform the committee of this fact. I am not asking for the details of the proposal but whether in fact the government will make any proposal to the conference along the lines I suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I think we will wish to know what the provinces have to propose in relation to formulas and in relation to all the other types of payments of which they are in receipt today. This conference will have to embrace consideration of the whole realm of payments whether conditional or unconditional.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The government has had two years in which to find that out from the provinces but I will leave that particular matter as it stands. Surely the minister, though he may not have read the statement from Mr. Frost which I mentioned, must be aware that some provinces are expressing views in this matter which if they were carried out would represent an additional contribution from the federal treasury and if these views were accepted by this conference in July it might be possible and indeed necessary to have a further amendment made to this legislation because we will undoubtedly be here at the time this conference is being held.


For instance, in an interview in Toronto with the editors of the Toronto Star just the other day, Mr. Frost had some interesting comments to make. I quote from the interview. He was asked about the federal-provincial fiscal conference called for July 6 and was asked the following question:
Templeton:	Can we go to another subject? On
the matter of the dominion-provincial fiscal conference which has been called for July 6, you have said that you expect to get a further $100 million at this conference-
Frost: That was dramatizing.
Templeton:	When you say you were dramatizing, are you suggesting that you don't mean it?
Frost: I certainly do mean it.
Further along Mr. Frost continued:
Our position is well known. As a major objective we have advanced the much-discussed 15-15-50 formula which means about $100 million to Ontario in new revenue.
We must assume from this that at least one province is going to put forward a formula, if that statement means anything at all. We have the right to assume also that this conference lasting for two days as the minister said, unless something intervenes to make it last longer, will then adjourn and after the two days a study is to be made of the whole question. Now we have the right to assume that the federal government after all these months is not itself putting forward any proposal for modification of this formula or for a new formula, beyond that which is embodied in the bill before us at this time.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to supplement what the Leader of the Opposition has just said and draw to the minister's attention the remarks he made at the close of the conference in 1957 as reported at page 102 of the proceedings:
Now, sir, may I make a brief comment on the suggestions as to the form in which the conference might continue.
I want to found a question on this, Mr. Chairman. I continue:
Suggestions were made yesterday on the part of two provincial premiers, I think, that an attempt should be made at this conference, which means today, to arrive at firm decisions. May I point out, sir-and I think this is in the minds of all of the provincial representatives-that we did call this conference as soon as possible after taking office. The new government has been faced with many burdens, including a number of conferences. This one was called as a two-day conference and the invitations were accepted on that basis.
Perhaps I might interject that two-day conferences seem to be the pattern. I continue:
The proposals which have been submitted-
In other words, in November of 1957, all these provinces made their proposals and now they are going to be asked at a lower level -I say this to justify my reference to the

forthcoming conference as a pale imitation of a conference-to come and repeat them, and still we have nothing from the federal government. I continue:
The proposals which have been submitted all involve the expenditure of large sums of money. All of them require careful study.
This is the Minister of Finance telling us how this thing was going to be done two years ago. It is very different from what he is telling us now. I continue:
Indeed, sir, we would be doing less than justice to them and the important sources from which they come if we did not undertake to give them careful study. Moreover, some of the proposals will necessarily involve extended planning and surveying before precise calculations could be arrived at or decisions based upon them.
That was a year and a half ago; a little more than that in fact. One question I should like to put at this time although I want to read a little more, is this. Would the minister tell us now what the result is of that planning and surveying and those precise calculations and what decisions have been based upon that year and a half of planning and surveying and precise calculating which he promised the premiers in November of 1957 he was going to do? I continue reading the minister's words at that conference: Therefore, in conclusion it seems to me that we are in this position. The provinces, which with one exception and one other exception in part, had entered into agreements with the former government effective on the first of April of this year, have in their statements indicated to us quite a marked difference in approach to the problem than one might have inferred from the signing of those agreements.
I should like to ask the minister, and this is the first time I have ever had the chance to do so, how he squares this statement with the statements he and the Prime Minister made before the election to the effect that this problem could be solved very simply by a single conference with all of the governments sitting down together and the conference reaching the agreements.
My second question to the minister is this. Is it intended that the conference in July should reach any conclusions or does the present government intend to treat this conference in exactly the same way as conferences have been treated by all governments since confederation, namely to listen to representations and then take its own responsibility before this house to this house, or does the minister think there is some other way of doing this? I think it is about time we had a precise answer to that question.
I return to the minister's remarks at the 1957 conference and continue reading:
Having regard to the extent, the number, the Importance and the cost involved In the various
Dominion-Provincial Relations important proposals which have been made, it Is evident, sir, as you said at the outset, that with a purse necessarily limited it is highly important that this conference should not close later today without our having gone as far as may be possible in seeking further information as to the views of the provinces concerning priorities among the various proposals put forward.
I think that after a year and a half the minister could perhaps tell us what those priorities are, what it is proposed to do first and what precise line the government now intends to take in this conference about the various proposals that were put forward at the last conference. I am sure that these ministers of finance are not just coming here for a joy ride. They want answers to these questions they put a year and a half ago. Personally, I know some of them expect answers and it seems to me that the minister could tell us what the general nature of those answers is going to be if, indeed, the government is going to put anything before this conference, or is the government just going to let the provincial governments make another series of requests and after two days send them home again? It seems to me that unless we are given a precise answer that is the inference we would draw.
I would remind the minister, in view of what he said a little earlier this afternoon, that when that series of five conferences which preceded the introduction by Mr. Harris of the present tax-sharing arrangements act was held, while no precise proposals were made by the federal government at the first and second of those meetings the federal government did give a very clear indication to the conference and to the public of the lines along which it was willing to approach this matter. In fact that approach was modified on at least three, and if my memory serves me rightly-I have not checked this carefully-or four occasions before the then prime minister and Mr. Harris made the statement they did. After four modifications, after four discussions with the provinces, where they were listened to and when many of their ideas were accepted, finally the government had to take its responsibility as finally this government perhaps will have to take its responsibility, though this government certainly has a great capacity for putting off until tomorrow those things that other governments used to do when problems were urgent. I ask the minister, does he intend merely to ask the provinces to come here again and make more speeches and then send them home, promising them still more study groups, or is the federal government going to give them any answers?
Before I resume my seat, and so that the minister can answer all my questions at

Dominion-Provincial Relations once, I should like the minister to tell me how much in total the provinces derived-I use the word "derived" because I know they did not receive it all from the federal treasury-because of the existence of the tax rental arrangements and the tax abatements in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1957, March 31, 1958 and March 31, 1959, without including the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant so that the figures will be strictly comparable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman began by reading remarks attributed to me in the record of the dominion-provincial conference of November 25 and 26, 1957, and the portion he read appeared to be treated by him as remarks made at the close of the conference with reference to some possible future meeting of the conference and the way in which the conference might continue. He quoted these words:
Now, sir, may I make a brief comment on the suggestions as to the form in which the conference might continue.
These remarks which the hon. gentleman has read from the record were not remarks made at the close of the conference at all. These remarks were made at the close of the public session on the morning of November 26 and were directed to the form in which the conference might proceed in the incamera session which followed upon the adjournment of the public session. My remarks related to the later meeting in camera on that day. They did not relate to some future resumption of a plenary conference.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Would the minister permit me to ask him a question so that we can clear up this point? The minister also remembers that there was a communique issued at the end of that conference and that communique contained these words with respect to taxsharing arrangements:
Possible changes in the tax-sharing arrangements act were discussed but it was understood that no endeavour would be made to reach conclusions on this matter prior to further consideration of the subject by the dominion government in the light of the public statements made by the provincial representatives in open sessions and the discussions which took place in committee.
Does the minister say that the consideration promised then is completed and that this measure is the result of it, or does he intend to deal further at the forthcoming conference with the rather strong demands that all provinces, without exception, made for a larger share of direct taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
There is no such thing as closing off demands on the part of any government in this field except to the extent to which the former government closed


them off by the terms of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act and the agreements that were entered into prior to March 31, 1957, in pursuance of the terms of that act.
The second question that the hon. member asked related to the purpose and scope of the conference, as I followed his remarks. Of course the provincial treasurers or ministers of finance are coming here with a serious purpose. We are going into this conference with a serious purpose and I stated that purpose this afternoon. We are making an earnest effort by means of the proposed co-operative approach and co-operative study to follow to make a thorough review of this field. Many, many questions have been raised from time to time in relation to this field and so far as we are able we intend to try to find long term solutions or settlements of the difficulties. That is the purpose of everyone. I have described in my remarks this afternoon the scope and purpose of the conference. These have been subscribed to by the provinces as evidenced by their acceptance of the invitation and the extent to which they have participated in the steps that have already been taken in preparation for the conference and the agenda for discussion.
The third matter the hon. member raised was as to the gross payments made-

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Gross advantage derived by the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: From payments made under this legislation or its predecessor?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: No, I should like figures to compare with those that the minister put in his budget papers. In other words, they would include either payments or tax abatements up to the amount because that is the only way you can get them comparable for the different provinces. I should like to have figures comparable with those which Mr. Harris gave when he introduced the measure originally in 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, excluding the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, the figures are as follows: For the fiscal year 1956-57, a total of $523 million; for 1957-58, $633 million; for 1958-59, $661 million, and that figure of course is subject to revision when the final figures are available. Then, for the present fiscal year, 1959-60, the estimate at this time is $753 million.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: $753 million-the minister estimates it is $100 million more this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: No, not $100 million, it is $92 million more, according to the present estimate.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Surely there must be some error in those figures because there is no difference in the formula this year from that for the year ending March 31, 1959.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: But there is a substantial difference in the tax returns estimated.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The minister will from those figures agree, I think, whatever may turn out to be the situation in 1960-I am sure he would also agree a large part of the returns from 1959-60 would have arisen under the old formula and that only the 3 per cent will come from the new formula- he will agree with me, I think-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I think the hon. member will agree, before he goes too far on that line, that had it not been for the amendment made last year to increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax, the yield to the provinces in 1958-59 would have been lower than the figure for 1957-58 because of the decline in the yield from personal income taxes, which would have brought into effect the wider application of the stabilization principle.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Was it not more a decline in the corporation tax? However, that is not really material. The point I am making here is that from the minister's figures it will be seen that the increase Mr. Harris proposed in 1956, and which came into effect for the fiscal year 1957-58, amounted to $110 million and this much boasted increase of this present government, which was going to be more generous, amounts to $29 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: No, that is not fair.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The figures are here. The minister has just given them. If the minister will subtract $523 million from $633 million, he will find that leaves $110 million. If he subtracts $633 million from $661 million, he will find that is $29 million. I have only done that mentally. I have not counted it on my fingers, but I think it is right, if the minister's figures are right. I am a little sceptical about the minister's figures because I think he told us in January, 1958, when he came into office and first told us about those telegrams of his in which he made other mistakes, that this was going to yield $62 million to the provinces. Now he tells us it is only $29 million.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It is $28 million.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The hon. member tells me it is only $28 million, and I think that is correct. I thank the hon. member for Halifax for making the minister's figures look even more absurd. Here is this great generosity
Dominion-Provincial Relations about which we have been told so much, this generosity about which the Minister of Justice went down to Newfoundland to tell the people, when a considerable portion of the total which he gave resulted from the action of Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris. I think it is time these facts were put before the public. This was the so-called take it or leave it attitude about which we heard so much, but the formula was actually the result of several conferences with the provinces in which many of their modifications were accepted and which yielded an additional $110 million. This operation by telegram turns out to have yielded $28 million, and I thank the hon. member for Halifax again for correcting my arithmetic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman professes to want facts.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Exactly, and I used only the minister's figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: He has proceeded from that to draw some very fictional conclusions. I think he had better add to his store of facts and draw the proper conclusions from them. It is true that in the year I have indicated, 1957-58, the payments to the provinces under this present act amounted to $633 million, but had we not introduced a year ago the amendment to increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax the provinces in the year 1958-59 would have received only $613 million, whereas they actually received, as a result of the legislation introduced by the present government, $661 million. In other words, they received $48 million more than they would have received under the former government if it had continued in office.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: That assumption, of course, is only an assumption; the hon. member does not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: This does not include the Atlantic adjustment grants. If you add the $25 million given under the Atlantic adjustment grants, it will be seen that the increased benefits to the provinces since this present government came into office, in the fiscal year 1958-59 by way of unconditional payments alone, were $73 million.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
It is still substantially less, even with that arithmetic by the minister, than Mr. Harris provided in 1956. I quite agree with the minister, and I never said anything to the contrary, that he did not do as well because the country did not do as well when he was in office as it did when Mr. Harris was in office; that is self-evident. The minister told the house in January, 1958,

Dominion-Provincial Relations that his best estimate was that this new arrangement would yield $62 million. He now says it yielded $48 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Yes, that was according to the estimates at that time.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: In other words, we have a pretty substantial shrinkage, even of the minister's $62 million. I wonder if the minister could tell us what the difference was between what Ontario actually got in 1958-59 under this arrangement and what Ontario would have obtained if this arrangement had not been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The payment in 1958-59 which Ontario would have received under the 10-9-50 formula would have been $71,786,000. The payment which it has received under the 13-9-50 formula was $93,322,000, an increase of $21,536,000 as a result of the amendment introduced a year ago.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It was about 10 per cent less than the minister estimated. I think his first estimate was about $23 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The figures I gave a year ago, I remind the hon. member, were given as illustrations based upon the figures for the previous year and such figures as were available at that time. We had not then arrived at the end or within several months of the end of the fiscal year 1957-58.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The minister also forgets he made a speech in the Montmagny byelection in which he gave solid figures that the people could count upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The figures I gave there, I think the hon. member will agree, according to the estimate made, were fair and proper.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The minister gave, in the by-election in October or September, whichever it was, the figures which he had given to the house in January, not a new estimate, which would have been lower.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Now that the minister's estimates have been checked against the facts, may I return to another aspect of this matter which we were discussing a few minutes ago? The minister has said something about the desirability of reaching long term solutions. I think we can all agree with that, in principle, though this bill is not a long term solution any more than was the bill last year. He also indicated that the conference to be called in July has a serious purpose. I am sure it has. The conference called on September 16, 1957, when he invited the provincial premiers to Ottawa in November, was meant to have a serious purpose. The

letter of invitation which can be read in Hansard at page 589 of that session, began as follows:
My colleagues and I believe it would be useful and desirable to arrange a dominion-provincial conference-
This was in September, 1957.
-to review the present pattern of tax-sharing arrangements.
That is a long time ago. At least it was one and a half years ago. At that meeting in November, as has been pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, at that two-day conference the federal government made some proposals and the provincial governments presumably made some proposals and the conference adjourned so that those proposals could be considered. It was understood that the conference would resume and deal with those proposals and presumably come to some long-term solution.
Now, a year and a half later, the minister says, "We are going to have another conference at which we are not making any proposals"-or at least he would not indicate to us on this side of the chamber that they had any proposals to make-"but at which we will consider once again the proposals which may be made by the provinces." That is what he told the provinces a year and a half ago, namely that they would consider the provincial proposals. Is this conference in July 1959 called for exactly the same purpose, namely to consider provincial proposals which were made a year and a half ago?
We know what some of those proposals were. It is an open secret. We know that some of the provinces want a 15-15-50 formula. Mr. Frost is going around the country saying that is what they are going to get in July. He did not say very much about it a year and a half ago and he did not say very much about it in the intervening period. But he has said a great deal about it in the last little while. Perhaps he has some basis for what he is saying. If he has, perhaps the minister might let us know. Perhaps his basis for it is the attitude of the Prime Minister in 1957 during the election when he campaigned with Mr. Frost and applauded Mr. Frost's demand at that time for a 15-15-50 formula. I do not think we should blame Mr. Frost too much if, in June, 1959, he feels he may be able to have this formula accepted.
But I ask the minister this question. Is that all that is going to happen in July, namely that the provinces are going to produce the old formula, or the old modifications and the government is going to have another look at it for another two days and set up a committee to have a further look at it during the next two years?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
When the minister was making his remarks a few minutes ago I intervened to ask a question but the minister thought it might be better dealt with at this time. The question I was going to ask had to do with the attitude taken by the minister with respect to the formula which was originally adopted by the former administration. The minister in his speech was extremely critical of that formula; that is, of course, the formula 10-9-50 which the present administration increased to 10-13-50 and is now seeking to extend for a further term.
But the point I wish to make at this stage is that while the minister was highly critical of our position and the attitude that was taken on this side of the house, I wonder whether he listened carefully to the speech made last evening by the hon. member for Bellechasse. The hon. member for Bellechasse was not nearly as critical of that attitude or that position as was the minister. I should like to refer him to what was said by the hon. member for Bellechasse as reported at pages 4304 and 4305 of Hansard. Of course, I am now paraphrasing his language but there he speaks of the conciliatory attitude of Mr. St. Laurent in dealing with this whole problem. He says that the formula and the principles laid down in the law known as 4-5 Eliz. II, chapter 29, to use his own expression: (Translation):
-reducing to silence the small politicians surrounding him, putting aside all narrow, mean and political considerations, became the instigator of "that law"-
(Text):
In other words, he commends the former prime minister for the attitude adopted in that formula. Later on, in another part of the speech he went on to defend that conciliatory attitude. I am therefore somewhat surprised at the fact that there seems to be a divergence of opinion. Perhaps I should not be surprised because that is something that often happens on the other side of the house, namely that the government is divided.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: My hon. friends shout "Oh, oh". We saw what happened with reference to the strike of the C.B.C. producers in Montreal. A portion of the government felt that the strike was legal and another portion felt that it was illegal.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that I am out of order; but I am out of order simply because I have been interrupted. I will now get back to what I intended to say and it is this. The attitude adopted by the minister and that adopted by the hon. mem-
Dominion-Provincial Relations ber for Bellechasse seem to be at variance and that is indicated from the language, as I see it, in Hansard. That leads me to this question. Has the minister received any representations since the 1957 conference from the premier of the province of Quebec or made representations with respect to this measure. What are his representations with respect to this agreement which is now before us? Is the premier satisfied with the division as it is found in this formula? I am sure the minister will want me to remind him that following the conference of 1957 the premier of the province of Quebec left the conference and said to everyone who wanted to listen how happy he was with the manner in which the proposals had been submitted and with the treatment that had been meted out to various groups; and he went on to repeat that for a period of some months. In fact, when he was chastised about his reversal of form, I think his words were something like this, "We must be patient; we must wait because it will take a long, long time for the present government to correct the many mistakes that were made by the former administration over a period of 22 years."
You can see, Mr. Chairman, how well that statement of the premier of the province of Quebec was received by those who applaud on the other side of the chamber. But have they seen or read or heard of the statement that he made only several months later on at least three occasions condemning, not in the most violent language-I do not think that is his attitude generally-but in the most vigorous language the conduct of the present government, and going so far as to say that it is even worse than was the conduct of the former administration.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: How could it be?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I believe that he used the words-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, is this relevant to the bill that is now before the committee?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister was allowed to roam all around section 12. Surely I may be allowed, as a preface to the questions that I intend to ask, to point this out. Surely I am entitled to point out a difference of opinion by one of the premiers of the provinces having to do with this kind of arrangement, an attitude which was entirely sympathetic in 1957 or shortly thereafter, and an attitude now which has been completely reversed and is in vigorous condemnation of the present attitude of the government. Before I proceed further, I ask the minister if he has received representations from the premier of the province of Quebec with reference to the formula which is now under discussion?

Dominion-Provincial Relations

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I take up the remarks made and questions put by the hon. member for Laurier before coming to the matters raised by the Leader of the Opposition. It is quite true the premier of Quebec expressed himself, I think it is fair to say, in laudatory terms of the atmosphere of the dominion-provincial conference of 1957. I know a great many of the delegates from the provinces expressed themselves to the same effect. They expressed the feeling that there was an entirely new atmosphere there quite different from the atmosphere which had prevailed in dominion-provincial conferences for some years prior to that time in view of the fact that there was no suggestion on the part of the federal government of any take it or leave it attitude, which marked a very strong change in the attitude of the federal government in 1957 as compared with the attitude of the federal government which had confronted them in previous conferences.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: That is not what Mr. Frost said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The hon. member for Laurier goes on from there to make statements about the attitude of the premier of the province of Quebec. I am not aware of any expressions of opinion on the part of the premier of the province of Quebec that jibe with those attributed to him by the hon. member for Laurier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The hon. minister had better read the newspapers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
It may be the
hon. member is better informed on the subject than I, but I have not seen remarks which tally with those attributed to the premier of Quebec by the hon. member for Laurier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The hon. minister is not up on the reading of his press clippings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
However, so far as his question is concerned I am not aware of any representations which have been made to us by the premier of Quebec with respect to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act or the division of yields between the dominion and provincial governments thereby provided.
So far as the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition are concerned, I think they left a quite unfair impression. He seemed to suggest that the dominion-provincial conference of November, 1957 had not been a fruitful conference. The fact is that it was a highly fruitful conference. It was from that conference that the efforts to work out a satisfactory formula for an Atlantic provinces adjustment grant ensued, which reached a happy conclusion in the voting by parliament
[Mr. Chevrier.!
of the sum of $100 million for the four Atlantic provinces over the period of four fiscal years.
In addition to that, Mr. Chairman, it was out of or in the course of that meeting when the provinces stated their needs, and in the light of those statements and the further representations which were made to us by the provincial treasurers in the ensuing weeks, particularly urgent in the light of their need to prepare their budgets for presentation to their legislatures early in 1958, that we asked the house to increase the provincial share of the yield from the personal income taxes from 10 to 13 per cent. That amendment of last year, as I have indicated already this afternoon, has brought very substantial benefits to the provinces. They are asking for a continuation of those benefits, and this measure which we are asking the house to endorse now is one which I think I can assure the house is being urgently and anxiously awaited by all provincial treasurers.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the minister's memory has failed him a little when he talked about the view taken at the conference in 1957 about a different attitude. I would like to read a little of what Mr. Frost said at this conference about Mr. St. Laurent. He said:
As I say I would like today again to voice my appreciation for his ability as chairman of several conferences and meetings and my thanks for the infinite patience-
I underline those words to the minister, and also the words "several conferences". It was not just a two-day shotgun affair, Mr. Frost continued:
-for the infinite patience he has invariably shown, for his unfailing courtesy which I think sprang from Mr. St. Laurent himself and from the fact that he is, basically, a Canadian gentleman and comes from that great race, two of the attributes of which are courtesy and understanding.
That is what the premier of the senior province said about Mr. St. Laurent and the way he conducted conferences when he was prime minister.
(Translation):

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) cannot answer for the premier of the province of Quebec, but everybody knows that the attitude of the province of Quebec is utterly negative and that, far from helping in anyway to settle this matter, the Quebec premier has always given a negative answer. At no time did he offer any serious alternative.
I have a question to ask and I should like to refresh the memory of the Minister of Finance. I shall even refer to the 50 Conservative members of this house who sup-

ported the attitude of the Quebec premier. Can the minister tell me if they have made any representations to him for a change in the principle of the act as passed by the former government. I shall get a bit closer still to the minister and ask him: Did the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), his colleague, make any representations requesting that this act which he said was unconstitutional, be made constitutional.
Moreover, in order to prove what I am saying, Mr. Chairman, I shall refer to a question and answer which appear on page 134 of the French edition of the official record of this house for 1957-58.
The member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, Mr. Maurice Breton, who was a good representative, said at that time:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. Solicitor General a question?
When sitting in the opposition the hon. Solicitor General has, on various occasions, given expression to the well-known thought that federal subsidies are unconstitutional. The opinion which he voiced then was shared in every way by the government of the province of Quebec. In view of the proposed federal-provincial meeting on fiscal matters, could he tell us now if he will oppose the subsidies which his government seems to be preparing at this time?
That was October 18, 1957, and Mr. Balcer answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell my hon. friend that I am still opposed to subsidies such as were proposed by the former government. As to his question, it seems to be a hypothetical one, but I am-

speechtext: A political one-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
-and a political one, yes. I want to tell him that the proposals of the federal government are not yet known, but I am convinced that they will be made on a very different basis from those of the former government.
According to the answer given me by the hon. Minister of Finance a moment ago, I must say that the only change that was made in this legislation is the amount of money given to the various provinces. It is not a question of dollars and cents that will make a legislation constitutional or unconstitutional. If the act was unconstitutional before the amount was raised, it is still so after any increase. Now because the Solicitor General had promised his voters that there would be a change-for in his view the wording of this legislation made it unconstitutional and a violation of provincial rights-he should have made representations to the Minister of Finance, as should also all Quebec members, urging him to change the principles and the basis of a legislation which, he alleged, was unconstitutional.
I see that the hon. Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) is smiling, but he has been more cautious than his
Dominion-Provincial Relations colleague the Solicitor General, because when asked the same question at that time, he refused to answer and preferred to wait until the government legislation was before the house. He did not wish to commit himself, because he knew very well that whatever reason he would give, he would have to follow the instructions of the head of the government.
Therefore, I ask the hon. Minister of Finance whether Quebec members, including the hon. Solicitor General, have made any representations to him? If so, why were not those representations favourably considered and why does the government come up with that selfsame act which had been adopted under the Liberal regime? In fact, only the amount has changed.
To say that granting 13 per cent instead of 10 per cent brings more money to each province is self-evident, and that is what was argued this afternoon. However, I should like to know whether the hon. minister has received any representations from the Solicitor General or from the Quebec members, and, if so, why those representations were ignored.
Mr. Chairman, I demand an answer. Yesterday, I was told that I kept silent on the matter. I find that if anyone should not remain silent, it is the Minister of Finance, considering that his own legislation is under review.
It is true I have not spoken every day for 22 years, but at least, I did not tell lies and I never tried to mislead people. When I spoke, I spoke the truth, and when I supported certain policies in election campaigns, I supported them in the house too. There have been times when I spoke and voted against my own party since, having promised my electors I would take a certain stand, I behaved accordingly. Therefore I am not like those people who rebuke me and who say in their constituencies that something is white and then say here in the house that it is black. Mr. Chairman, I should like to get a reply from the Minister of Finance before he is accused of being speechless as I was accused recently. It seems to me it should be easy to know, Mr. Chairman, whether the minister has received any representations from Quebec members for a change in the principles of this legislation.

Under the formula as it was first enacted, 9 per cent of corporation profits go to the provinces, while 38 per cent of these profits are assigned to the federal government. It follows from that that the proportion received by the provinces is 24 per cent of that received by the federal government. That is under the old system. maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we were interrupted by the arrival of Black Rod I was just at the beginning of a question to the minister and I think I had gone so far as pointing out that the question was asked at the resolution stage by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. The minister will recall that on April 20 the Prime Minister, on the television network program "The Nation's Business", made a statement in which he said:
In the very careful study which I have been giving to this whole matter, I find that since confederation Newfoundland has received a total of $300 million from the federal government, including the amounts for the current year.
Then he went on to show how this $300 million was made up. My hon. friend asked that comparable totals be given for all the provinces. The minister will recall also that a starred question was asked by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception requesting not merely the total but also breakdowns for the other three Atlantic provinces and for Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and that question was made an order for return before this debate began. I do believe, in view of the fact that these figures have been given and that the Prime Minister claimed on TV he had made a careful study of the matter, that comparable figures should be given. Obviously, the Prime Minister would not have said he had made a careful study of this matter if he had not compared the Newfoundland figures with the other figures. I would not suggest for a moment that the Prime Minister would have obtained the figures for Newfoundland and, without relating them in any way to the other provinces, put them forward as though they were something startling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
It should be noted, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. gentleman takes his starting point, not from anything said

in the course of the debate on this measure at its various stages but rather from what the Prime Minister said during a television broadcast. What was referred to there embraced a great deal more ground, of course, than the bill now before the committee. It embraced not only the unconditional payments provided for under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, but all manner of conditional payments that the federal treasury contributes to the assistance of the provinces.
It is quite obvious that the type of material now sought is quite outside the scope of this measure and outside the scope of the present debate. This does not mean that the hon. gentleman cannot possibly obtain the information he wishes. As a matter of fact, there was an order of this house passed some days ago which, in its scope, embraced as I understand it the information now sought by the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Some of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The information the hon. gentleman is seeking could be had at any time in the proper way. It is not relevant to this measure now before the committee. The hon. gentleman can certainly have the information. When it was requested I indicated it was not available then. The information, so far as it was within the possession of the finance department, was compiled in response to the order for return passed by the house, and that will be forthcoming in the ordinary course. It includes much that is quite outside the scope of the present measure.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I must say, Mr. Chairman, there certainly seems to be in the opinion of the minister, one rule for one side of the house and one for the other, because in his speech closing the debate on second reading he made very considerable reference, without giving precise figures, to this very subject. It seems to be all right for the minister to traverse all kinds of ground but when anyone on this side of the house attempts to obtain information, then he is told it is outside the scope of the bill.
The purpose of this legislation is to increase the amounts the provinces will receive under the tax-sharing arrangements. It is hard to conceive of anything that could be more relevant, if we are to give proper consideration as to whether this is the right amount or the adequate amount, than knowing what the total amount is that the provinces have received.
There is another reason for asking for this information. The Prime Minister said he had given very careful study to this
Dominion-Provincial Relations matter. The Minister of Justice went down to Newfoundland and gave figures on the same subject which turned out to be hopelessly incorrect, and which he said he obtained from the Department of Finance. This whole information relating to Newfoundland has, in our opinion, been used to create an entirely illusory impression on the public. We do believe, when we consider this problem of federal-provincial financial relations, that we are entitled to the information for all the provinces.
The minister says we can get this. My hon. friend from Trinity-Conception put a starred question on the order paper a week after this broadcast was delivered, that is to say late in April, and it is now June 4 but we have not received this information yet. It is all very well for the minister to say that we can get this information. It is true that we can put motions on the order paper; it is true we can put questions on the order paper which are then made orders for returns and are buried in the department of the Secretary of State, which seems literally to have become a burial ground for these returns. If the rules permitted me, I would say that I do know the department has this information. I know it would not take the minister two minutes, if he has brought them with him from the department, to produce the figures giving the comparable totals for all the provinces. I know this because I used to be a member of the government and, from time to time, I used to get this information. It did not take two months to get it, either. I cannot believe that the machinery of government has broken down quite to that extent in the two short years the hon. gentleman has been presiding over the Department of Finance, although we know there has been a very sad deterioration. I do suggest the minister would facilitate the passage of this legislation by giving this information here and now.
