maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I have another point that I want to take up, since I take it we are going to be denied this information. We are told we can get it, but it seems to be impossible to get it when you ask for it. The minister also talked about the beautiful harmony that had been established between the federal government and the provinces since this government came into office. When the hon. member for Laurier suggested that perhaps this harmony, in so far as the government of Quebec was concerned, is not as great as it seemed to be two years ago, the minister said he had not read anything to indicate the contrary.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I happen to have right here in my hand a clipping from one of the minister's favourite newspapers, Le Devoir, for April 2 of this year-I shall not quote this because it is not directly on the point-in which the premier of Quebec took the most violent exception to action taken by this government. This is only one of many that we could furnish.
But it is not only with the government of Quebec that we have this new harmony. Last week in another debate we witnessed-and I am not going to traverse it-the Prime Minister making attacks on the governments of two provinces in a single speech. That is something that did not use to happen when we were in office. I never, during the time that Mr. St. Laurent was in office, heard him make any attack on any provincial government, whatever the provocation.
If the hon. gentleman thinks his government has good relations with the province from which I happen to be elected, I think perhaps he is unique in holding that view. The fact of the matter is that since this government came into office there has been a most shocking deterioration in the relations between the federal government and the governments of the provinces. Part of the reason for that deterioration is that the provinces and the public were told in 1957 that a Conservative government would solve this problem at a single conference. Instead of that, we have this one year at a time business.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, why do we have this bill brought back every year? The Leader of the Opposition pointed out quite clearly this afternoon that this government has not any intention of doing anything more than this for the currency of these agreements. Why does not the minister ask right here and now to amend this bill in committee and at least spare us this annual agony until 1962? He is not ever going to do any more and he knows it perfectly well. Mr. Frost is not going to get one nickel-and let the minister remember that phrase; he is not going to get five cents-of his hundred million dollars from this government; not five cents of it. This camouflage about this pale imitation conference, for which this government-as the minister admitted this afternoon -has no program at all, no agenda, no proposals, is all we have.

I would not like, Mr. Chairman, to irk the minister, especially today when he has just been appointed Secretary of State for External Affairs, but just the same, I hope, he will harbour no hard feelings against me if I use the very phrases he used with regard to us last year. In my opinion, it would be wise to remark here that the minister became quickly out of breath since within a single year the percentage of efficiency suffered a substantial decline. We can also infer that if in 1957-58, 97 per cent of the appropriations had been spent, this was undoubtedly due to the fact that most of the projects implemented during that year had been prepared by the former Liberal administration.
I have drawn up a table which gives us a rather good idea of the degree of efficiency in the Department of Public Works during the fiscal year 1958-59. After adding up the appropriations in the main and in the supplementary estimates, I compared them with the expenditures which were made during the year which are shown in table 26, on page 65 of the budget papers tabled in the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on the occasion of his budget speech.
Under the heading "Public Buildings- construction and services-Acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings", we find that an amount of $25.1 million was voted while $19.8 million were spent, that is a percentage of 78.9 per cent.
For other centres in Canada, outside of Ottawa, $43.4 million were voted, while $34.1 million were spent, that is a percentage of 78.6 per cent.
Under the item "Harbours and Rivers Engineering Services-Acquisition, construction and improvements of harbour and river works", we notice that $37.2 million was voted while $27.3 million was spent, that is, a proportion of 73.4 per cent.
And now, under the item "Development Engineering Services,-Trans-Canada Highway-Construction through National parks", which comes directly under the jurisdiction of the department of the federal government, $12.5 million were voted, while $10 million were spent. The proportion there is 80 per cent.
So we can realize that the degree of efficiency with regard to those various items, which concern construction more particularly, varies from 67.3 per cent to 80 per cent.

It is indeed strange, under the circumstances which existed in 1958-1959, having in mind the record number of unemployed at the time, that the Department of Public Works spent $22.8 million less than provided for in the estimates. It might be worth noting that, in fact, the expenses of the department for the year ending March 31, 1959, increased by only $14 million as compared with 1957-58.
Mr. Chairman, we found that we were very far from the glittering promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in February 1958, when he was talking of his great special public works program to the amount of $1,185,000,000. Canadians, during the last fiscal year, have fully realized that that program was nothing but window dressing and represented only the normal expenditures of the government departments and agencies, plus some investments by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PUBLIC WORKS

Now let us take this year's estimates, the estimates for 1959-60. It would be a good thing to point out that the estimates for the current year, as listed in the blue book, show a decrease of $18,665,715 in construction of public buildings and of $5,692,300 for harbours and rivers, thus bringing the total decrease to more than $24 million.
The supplementary estimates are not all known as yet but, judging from past experience, the supplementary estimates for the Department of Public Works usually amount to $14 or $16 million. We would then have, under these two important headings, a decrease of $8 to $10 million, including the supplementary estimates that will come later.
In fact, Thursday, May 21, the minister said that the estimated amount required for the year 1959-60 was $173.6 million, or $17.8 million less than the previous year. The minister indicated at that time that he was hoping that no one would criticize him for having reduced the expenditure. However I hope he does not expect us to congratulate him. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, this substantial decrease seems very strange to me, and I wonder what causes it. Would it be that the projects that the Minister of Public Works mentioned last year, when he introduced his budget last May 21st, are not ready? Yet he told us at that time, as found in Hansard of June 6, 1958, page 907, and I quote:

We intend to build up a proper shelf of public works which can be called on immediately.
Or is it that the treasury board, under the leadership of the hon. Minister of Finance, is too strict? However that is not what he said-I am referring to the Minister of Finance-that is not what he implied when he said the following, which can be found in Hansard of January 21, 1958, page 3569, and I quote:
Let me make it abundantly clear to every member of the house-I made this clear in the financial statement I made in the house on December 6

that the instructions that have been given by the government are to the effect that while we are seeking to reduce expenditure where expenditure is needless we have said that there shall be no reduction in expenditure where it means jobs, and we are seeking to increase construction in useful public works down the line. While next year we would unquestionably like to have a balanced budget, let me make it abundantly clear that we are not going to put a balanced budget above our firm determination to provide, through the agency of public works, jobs for unemployed Canadians.
Well, Mr. Chairman, committee members must certainly find it rather strange that the estimates of the Department of Public Works should be reduced in a year, when, as late as last April, according to statistics, there were more than 445,000 unemployed while, according to statistics supplied by the national employment service, there are 733,000 registered applicants looking for a job.
It seems that the government has been so dazzled by the "vision" it had before the election that it is unable to realize exactly the prevailing situation.
I feel that, instead of reducing estimates assigned to job-making construction projects, the Department of Public Works should have increased them. Thus, the minister would have been consistent, especially in view of the statements he made last year. But again we note that the government does not seem to be taking any action that would make unemployment less severe next winter than it was last winter.
Again, like last year, municipalities will no doubt be saddled with the responsibility of finding work for hundreds of thousands of unemployed. In my opinion, we would be justified in saying that we have heard a lot of empty talk from the government but we have not seen much action, that we have heard many promises, but that few have been fulfilled.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Public Works inherits a tradition that finds its genesis in the mist of antiquity. I find on reading that throughout the ages it has been primarily concerned with mortar and water in its various forms. I think it is safe to say that the first well known public work was Noah's ark which was used to rescue mankind from the flood. The second best known public work was the tower of Babel which caused the confusion of mankind in a flood of languages. And so on down through the ages until we come to Canada's best known edifice, the printing bureau, built on a flood as the result of a freshet of errors and a cataract of public expenditure. History abounds with similar errors caused by ignorance and in some cases by cupidity. Fortunately, however, it is replete with illustrations that some person always came forward to take corrective measures to remedy these situations.
Some years ago Mr. Blair Fraser, Ottawa editor of Macleans magazine said in his column, which incidentally is read by thousands of people across Canada, "the public works department is the last patronage swamp to be drained". I am of the opinion that Mr. Fraser was a little too optimistic at that time. I think there are a few stagnant

Supply-Public Works
pools in the post office and transport departments, but even those pools are being drained to a certain extent and are in a much better condition in recent years.
A great many people in Canada agreed with Mr. Fraser's statement and a great number of people within the party that was in power at that time felt a general dissatisfaction with the public works department. I am told it was overloaded in the postwar years and that the organization was inefficient and insufficient. A great many people looked for action to remedy the situation.
You know, Mr. Chairman it is remarkable how history repeats itself-even in public works. It is known that the Assyrians and Nebuchadnezzar relied on the astrologers, astronomers and the generals, I find from a reading of history, for the planning of buildings, the building of canals and the building of gardens in the valley of the Euphrates. The Pharaohs, I find on reading history, used their generals to organize the labour required to build the pyramids. Napoleon consulted with his engineers and generals when drawing plans for a new and more beautiful Paris that could be easily defended against invaders.
In 1952 the Canadian government realized that the public works department required some reorganization and improvement. I think because of that realization the Hon. Robert Winters, an engineer, was appointed as the minister. I think all hon. members will agree he was a most capable minister. It was not long before he made history repeat itself. He began to look around the Canadian landscape and appointed a former quartermaster general of the Canadian army as his deputy. They both commenced a reorganization of the department with vigour and dispatch.
We were very pleased with this reorganization. The effect of the appointment of the former minister, the Hon. Robert Winters, and of the present deputy minister was soon noticed in the department and by the results obtained. We were extremely pleased because for years we in this group have been advocating planning in all government activities and in the economic organization of our country. We have taken a strong stand against patronage.
To be quite fair it is much easier to take a strong stand against patronage when you are not in power than when you are in power but we have always taken this stand throughout the years. I can see a certain sympathetic smile in response to that remark on the lips of the minister at this time.
[Mr. Herridge.l
As a result of the efforts of the two gentlemen to whom I referred the draining of the patronage swamp mentioned by Mr. Fraser was nearly completed. I think there are a few odds and ends to be cleared up yet mostly found among lower paid employees and casuals. I am not blaming the senior officials for that nor am I blaming the minister. It is very difficult to have your finger on every little thing that is happening in a department that carries on such large scale operations as does the Department of Public Works.
In 1957 the present minister was appointed and gave the "Green" light-large capital and small letters-for continued efforts to improve the efficiency and planning procedures of the department. This was no easy task, with his party out of office for 22 years. We are all human and, without a doubt, the minister was faced with the long time habits of certain persons who had been used to giving first consideration to Liberal members or defeated Liberal candidates and other persons influential with the party in power. That is a situation that takes some time to correct in fairness and properly. And then, there is always a minority when a party has been out of office that long that wants to feed from the nose bag of patronage.
I want to say right here that I have had something to do with the federal Department of Public Works throughout the years, on one occasion as a conscript employee, and on another as a close observer of a great deal of their work in my constituency, and as a friend of a great many of the officials going back over 50 years. The minister deserves great credit for his demonstration of his consistency, integrity and industry in the administration of his department and his unfailing courtesy to all members, regardless of party.
There is a tradition of public works in the minister's family. I remember the minister's uncle when he was a member of the provincial legislature of British Columbia. He was the first member responsible for getting a few miles of road built in that part of the constituency in which we live. He was responsible for getting the Sandon flume built after the big fire of 1900. He was interested in that. I know that in the early days he was active in public works which were of great concern to everyone in a country lacking roads, communications and so on.
This improvement in departmental organizations would be impossible without the cooperation, professional and administrative ability of the deputy minister, of the senior officials in Ottawa and the district officials and staff throughout the country. I think we should give credit to those who are in quite

minor positions across Canada and who carry-on their valuable work from year to year. I know that in the past some have received little sympathy or understanding from headquarters in Ottawa about the problems they have to face from day to day.
We in this group appreciated the minister's statement as to policy, planning and with respect to expenditures. He gave quite an adequate and informative synopsis of the proposals and activities of his department. We were interested in hearing about the proposals with respect to the trans-Canada highway. I was particularly interested in hearing about the program for the building of small, standard post offices throughout the country, which I think will receive unanimous approval. I found an excellent response in my own constituency to this planning ahead for the placement of these small post offices in villages and other locations. This brings the people of the smaller places in closer touch with the activities of the federal government, and I think it gives them a certain esprit de corps.
I happen to know that there is to be a building of that type built in a little village near where I live, in Nakusp. It is the first public building of its kind in that village, and it is very much appreciated. It will be a beautiful building and is situated in a pretty village. The erection of these small buildings in these smaller places, which serve the needs of the people in the smaller places which I think have been somewhat overlooked in the past, is excellent. I think it is an excellent program and is well planned ahead. I like the minister's idea of obtaining the sites upon which buildings can be erected at a time when that will be of the greatest advantage in aiding local unemployment.
I was interested also, in the minister's statement with respect to the co-operation of the research council, and the very sensible use of models to study all the considerations connected with large projects, particularly when the effect of water has to be considered. I think that is a very worth-while step indeed. I was interested in his statement with respect to the maintenance and repair of public buildings in the winter months, as I said before to the best advantage in meeting any local unemployment situation.
The C.C.F. believes that sound planning is required to secure the best value from the expenditure of public funds. It is obvious that the senior officials of this department have brought a great deal of order out of the former chaos as a result of planning since 1952. For instance, if you read the
Supply-Public Works
departmental report for 1952 you will find that it provides for reports from the deputy minister, the chief architect, the chief engineer, the treasury officer and the chief of legal services. I am not criticizing the organization of years ago which, before expenditures were so large, possibly was adequate.
We are very glad now, however, to note that under the supervision of the former minister and the present minister, and under the guiding hand of the deputy minister and his senior officials, the reorganization of the Department of Public Works has produced results. I have noticed that in this year's report, instead of reports from the few people I have mentioned in the 1952 report, we now have reports on departmental activities broken down into the harbours and rivers engineering branch, the development engineering branch, building construction branch and property and building management branch. In my opinion it was a very wise move to establish the property and building management branch. Then, we have the purchasing and stores branch, the administrative services and secretary, the economic studies branch, which is a very important thing particularly when expenditures are proposed for wharves or public buildings.
It is then necessary that the department have some idea of the future possibilities with respect to the development of the area in which the money is going to be expended. There have been occasions in the past when considerable sums of money were spent because the department lacked the economic studies branch and the economic activity of the community in which the expenditure was made declined very shortly after the building, wharf or public project was constructed.
Then we have the report of the financial services, information services, legal services, the personnel branch and so on. The reading of this report, and the breakdown into the various departments, gives one a clear indication that the department is well planned, well organized and in a position to undertake the large responsibilities that it has to accept at this time and the increasing responsibilities that will come throughout the years.
I should like to make a few suggestions before concluding, and I am only making a few general remarks on the administration item. We in this group believe that planning should be some years ahead, so far as possible, concerning prospective needs. We believe that the economic studies branch should be supplying the deputy minister and the minister with information that will allow them to get a very clear picture of the likely developments in any area, say, for the coming

Supply-Public Works
10 years. I believe that this is necessary in order to plan properly and to have projects, as it were, on the shelf to be undertaken at any time to meet a local unemployment situation.
I should like to say a word or two about public relations. In my opinion public relations are a very important part of any federal government department's activities. Naturally, the ministers travel around the country and make occasional speeches at certain centres. The more they do of that, the better. But I am suggesting that even the deputy minister and some of the senior officials should have the opportunity of meeting and addressing representative public bodies such as chambers of commerce or, on occasion, ladies' organizations or trade unions, so that more and more people will get some idea of the organization and activities of the public works department of Canada for which they pay.
In addition to that, I think there should be developed as much communication as possible between district officials, local officials and local organizations. I say that even the local organizations in the smallest places should be given an opportunity to be informed of the department's plans, as to whether they are going to demolish a wharf, erect a building or where they are going to do some particular work. From my experience I have found that when the public, particularly in the smaller places, are consulted or matters are discussed-mind you, I know the department is responsible for making the final decisions-you build up a spirit of good will and you get the co-operation of the local people. I have this slight criticism, that I think on some occasions the department, possibly through lack of complete knowledge of changed conditions and circumstances, has decided to do something at the district office level without complete understanding of the local situation. I do urge that the minister's district officers and his local officials do everything possible to get the co-operation of and to consult representative local organizations.
Then I suggest it would be a good idea for the department to issue releases to the local press concerning any particular work. I think this would avoid a lot of rumours and misunderstanding about such things as the site, the date when construction is expected to commence, and so on. That is news to people, especially in the smaller places. Possibly it is not news to people in the larger places because their minds are occupied with all forms of gaiety and other activities, but in the country where people are generally more serious, somewhat more stable, they are interested in local business or local public

buildings or a local wharf, and so on. I suggest there could be an extension of the practice of issuing press releases in the area so that people are kept well informed on the activities of the department, what it intends to do and when it intends to do it. In my opinion an informed public with respect to any department of government is a cooperative public. When it comes to administration all departments of government in a democratic society must seek to promote, in my opinion, the understanding and the cooperation of the people they aim to serve.
I have one other suggestion and it is this. Because of the vast areas that district engineers must serve I believe that senior officials, particularly in the district offices, should not be moved too frequently. It takes two or three years for a district engineer, for example, who serves the British Columbia and Yukon district to get to know the district he serves. He cannot be travelling all the time. He has a great deal of administrative responsibility. I suggest that senior officials should not be moved too frequently, that is at the district office level. I also hope that the minister's department is undertaking plenty of planning and that its economic studies branch is feeding the senior officials with information that will provide them with the opportunity to plan for the department to play its full role and part in meeting any unemployment situation that should occur in the winter ahead.
I have made a few general remarks with regard to general administration. I have some other matters to raise with regard to public buildings, construction and services, harbours and rivers engineering service branch and trans-Canada highway. At that time I shall leave the general and move to the particular. What I have to say will also include a few pleas on behalf of the constituents whom I have the honour to represent.

If I had been in a mood to echo that particular remark, it had as its intention an indication of disappointment perhaps that there would not be an expression from the house leader, that these estimates would now be passed in order to allow the new minister to go on to his new duties. My own reaction was disappointment. I have always looked forward to hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Levis. As remarkable as are the simultaneous translators here tonight, something is always lost in the translation.
If ever a man's head might be turned in my brief experience in this house, it certainly would be the head of the Minister of Public Works and now Secretary of State for External Affairs by the glowing tributes paid to him by the two opposition parties today on two separate counts. Those of us on the government back benches by our applause expressed our opinion concerning the events that took place at the beginning of the proceedings today. I think it would be remiss indeed if some expression of our opinion were not given concerning the former Minister of Public Works, although I am not just quite sure whether I am correct in that designation. He has left his imprint-and I am sure it will be a lasting one-on the job he is leaving. I would agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West in putting at the head of a list his courageous and tenacious attitude concerning the matter of patronage. This is something that has certainly required tenacity, stick-to-it-iveness and other similar qualities.
We have heard of the tremendous team spirit developed in the department. While most of us backbenchers have not been too familiar with the workings of that department, we can certainly understand how that team spirit should develop under the leadership of the minister. The extension of the tender system is part of the reflection of his attitude and his philosophy in connection with patronage which are well known. The imprint of which I spoke a few moments ago can be seen in the extension and expansion of public works and the co-operation of the department. But mostly, Mr. Chairman, I would think it would be the greatest source of satisfaction when leaving this portfolio to realize the tremendous number of young persons, young family people in this country who own their own homes, a situation attributable in no small number to the efforts of the Minister of Public Works.
This applies through the field of housing and one in particular in which I am interested and which I know a great many members share this view, namely that of limited
Supply-Public Works
dividend housing. Thousands and thousands of extra units are now available on a low rental basis to people who desperately need that accommodation. This will not be quickly forgotten by those people or those of us in whose ridings these developments have taken place. As I say, it must be a great source of satisfaction to the minister to leave that kind of an imprint on his department as he leaves.
But mostly, Mr. Chairman, and again I speak for the younger members in the house -I speak of the example that he has set for us in the performance of his duties in this house and in our caucus, his reform instincts, his integrity and his availability- and that has been mentioned by both opposition parties-not only to those on the government benches but to each and every member of the House of Commons. I have no wish to prolong the discussion on the estimates. I simply felt that this expression should be made not only on behalf of the G.F.A.- which, I may say, for the benefit of the group in the corner is a group of nine members in this area. We in this group should like to congratulate the minister and wish him the very best in the future.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with all those who have congratulated the minister on his new portfolio and to wish him well in his new sphere of activities. I am sure most of us today heard the Prime Minister's announcement with mixed feelings. While we rejoice with the minister at this broader scope for his undoubted talents and ability, nevertheless I think most of us felt a little bit sad-perhaps it was a selfish sadness -on losing from the portfolio of minister of public works a man who has won our utmost admiration, not only for his integrity but for the outstanding non-partisan manner and approach which he has always displayed in dealing with all our problems.
Personally, I want to thank him most sincerely for the sympathetic and kind consideration which he has always given to the problems which I have brought before him. In that I should like to include a tribute to his staff, not only here in the head office at Ottawa but also those who serve in the district office in Newfoundland. The minister is fortunate in having a most competent staff who are always anxious to do everything possible to help out with the problems of our province, and the only remark I should like to make about them is that I think they are perhaps the most overworked staff in the whole civil service of Canada, and possibly the most underpaid as well.

Supply-Public Works
It is nice, of course, to have a minister who is kind and sympathetic to our problems, but we know that with all the goodwill in the world he must still get his expenditures authorized by the treasury board. The minister does not have the last say as to what expenditures will be made. Last year the Minister of Finance who presides over the treasury board allayed our fears when he stated, as reported on page 3569 of Hansard for January 21, 1958:
Let me make it abundantly clear to every member of the house-I made this clear in the financial statement I made in the House on December 6- that the instructions that have been given by the government are to the effect that while we are seeking to reduce expenditure where expenditure is needless we have said that there shall be no reduction in expenditure where it means jobs, and we are seeking to increase construction in useful public works down the line. While next year we would unquestionably like to have a balanced budget, let me make it abundantly clear that we are not going to put a balanced budget above our firm determination to provide, through the agency of public works, jobs for unemployed Canadians.
Since then the Minister of Finance seems to have undergone a change of heart, because on April 21 he made another statement in this house which was quite different from the one which I have just quoted. This is what the Minister of Finance said on that occasion, as reported on page 2889 of Hansard:
The treasury board this year has been tighter and closer in its scrutiny of estimates than ever before. A lot of these things are not talked about in detail everywhere, but let there be no doubt about it; the treasury board today is doing an effective piece of work.
Then the minister ended the paragraph with these words:
There is a tightening of the rein on expenditures.
As long as the present Minister of Public Works held his portfolio these words did not chill our hearts quite as much, because we had confidence that the benign influence which we know the minister exercises over his colleagues would have an effect in softening the hard hearts of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues on the treasury board. But now that the minister is leaving this portfolio I think our fears have been renewed that his successor might not have that benign influence and that we may perhaps not receive as sympathetic consideration as we have in the past. We hope the Prime Minister will take these qualities into account when he appoints the new minister of public works.
The tightening up which the Minister of Finance referred to on April 21 is shown in the main estimates for this year. On page 67 we notice that there is an over-all decrease in expenditures of $14,900,293. Even when

we subtract from that the $4 million in the supplementary estimates, we still have an over-all decrease of over $10 million. But the tightening up of expenditures is most marked when we consider the items of public buildings, construction and services and the items under the heading of harbours and rivers engineering services. There is a decrease in expenditure of over $19 million for public buildings and a further $5 million nearly under the heading harbours and rivers, making a total decrease of around $24 million. Even when we deduct the $3 million plus under these two headings in the supplementary estimates, we still have a decrease in expenditure of over $20 million.
I think it is unfortunate that these decreases have occurred under these particular headings, because they happen to be the very headings which provide jobs. We already have on our hands a substantial amount of unemployment, and I think it is reasonable to expect that the unemployment problem will be with us again next year, and a reduction under these headings is certainly going to aggravate that problem instead of alleviate it.
In my own province in Newfoundland we feel this very acutely, because under these two headings of harbours and rivers and public buildings, construction and services, there is an over-all reduction of nearly $2.8 million, which in a province that depends on public works for supplementary earnings is quite substantial. 1 know that part of this reduction has been brought about because many of the large projects in our province have now been taken care of. We also know that it is impossible to counteract this amount of expenditure under the housing program. Therefore, I should like to sound this warning to the Minister of Public Works and to his successor in office, that they keep this in mind when they are preparing the estimates for next year, because very drastic reductions under these two headings are going to cause some degree of hardship in my province.
Mr. Chairman, there are one or two other aspects of the estimates about which I would like to comment. First of all, I would like to commend the minister for the increase in the miscellaneous grants. This grant has been increased by $750,000 and that is particularly welcome in my province because, as I have said, most of the heavy works have now been completed and in the future there is going to be a larger and larger number of small works costing less than $25,000 which by law will have to be financed out of this miscellaneous grant. I thank the minister for this increase and I hope that next year's estimates will show a further increase.

I wish also to thank the minister for the increase shown under the heading "dredging, construction and acquisition of plants and equipment." One of our most urgent needs in Newfoundland is dredging. As we know, private dredging companies are still very busy and it is most difficult to get the kind of plant that we need. The minister may remember that last year I pointed out to him that we have a special need for shallow dredging equipment for the dredging of shallow harbours. We have none of that equipment being operated by the department in Newfoundland at the present time, and I hope that part of this vote will be used to acquire this type of dredging equipment.
Before I sit down, I wish to draw the attention of the minister to one very small problem. When small works are undertaken in small fishing settlements in my province-[DOT] works such as the building of a wharf or breakwater-the common practice is to acquire the rocks required for the ballast by contract. That is possibly a very businesslike way of handling this requirement but it has one serious drawback for my people, because when the fishermen pick up these rocks and sell them under contract they do not receive unemployment stamps. Had they been able to get these stamps last year many of them would have qualified, taking into account the stamps they receive while fishing, for seasonal benefits. I would ask the minister to take this into consideration and perhaps give a direction so that the department may acquire this material by day labour instead of by contract.
Like everyone else here I wish the minister the very best of success in his new undertaking.

I do not mean to delay the committee with many remarks I should like to make at this time with regard to the announcement which was made in the early afternoon. I know that the people of Canada will have heard the news with great happiness and satisfaction, and I know that particularly the people in the minister's home area in British Columbia will take a special delight in the announcement. I know that with elections coming hard and heavy for a number of years in Canada, Canada's position throughout the world has not continued recently to grow as we had been led to believe it might, and I know the minister will at an early date do much to enhance Canadian prestige abroad in the interest not only of world peace but of our economic interest as well.
All of us are deeply concerned about who the new minister of public works may be. We hope and trust he will be some one who 66968-9-277
Supply-Public Works
will have an integrity equal to that possessed by the hon. gentleman who now holds that office.
I should like to make an appeal to the minister with regard to a number of issues, because I believe the hon. gentleman has a number of headaches which have still to be cleared up and I should like to see him make an effort to handle these difficult matters before he leaves his present office. The main question to which I should like the minister to give some attention is the problem facing us with regard to interest rates on loans for homes which are now being built and which will be built during the months and years ahead under the National Housing Act.
The minister realizes very well that interest rates under the National Housing Act are determined in the long run by the rates which the government has to pay on long term government issues of bonds, and as I understand it the yield on long term government issues or bonds at the present time is practically as high as the maximum interest rate allowed under the National Housing Act. The minister indicates that this is not the case. But even a one year issue yesterday returned a yield to the investors of 5.49 per cent. If a one year issue is able to produce a yield of 5.49 per cent, we must remember that it has always hitherto been assumed that long term issues return a higher yield and therefore any money which the government will have to borrow in the months ahead to lend to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will have to be supplied to this crown corporation at a very high rate indeed, and the margin between even 5J per cent and 6 per cent is a very narrow one. The act allows for a margin up to 2 per cent.
The minister has let us know that the government has no intention of raising the allowable interest under the National Housing Act, and we were happy to hear that announcement. However, the minister announced in no uncertain terms some months ago that the government had no intention whatsoever of allowing the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to operate at a loss, and we are unable to reconcile the two statements. If the government intends to maintain the maximum allowable rate of interest at 6 per cent, then we believe the government will have to look things squarely in the face and admit that it may well be necessary in the public interest to agree to subsidize the operations of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There simply is no other way out of this predicament. I believe the minister would agree that the situation is a difficult one. I know he does not like having to advise any branch of the government that it

Supply-Public Works
will be allowed to operate at a deficit. However, here I believe is a situation where an understanding of that kind will have to be reached, otherwise I am afraid that that organization, belonging to the pepole, will be unable to discharge its responsibilities adequately.
The other headache which must concern the minister and about which I hope some action can be taken is the amount of money which is available for housing or which it appears will be available for the purpose of housing. The returns from many other enterprises are so much higher now that there is a little less interest or, I should say, there is a lot less interest on the part of those who have investment money available to make such money available for housing at the 6 per cent gross level.
I believe that action will have to be taken and it may have to be rather strong action compared with any action that has been taken hitherto. I agree wholeheartedly that maximum interest rates should not be raised. However, it is equally vital that sufficient money for housing be made available and I am wondering whether consideration of amendments to the Bank Act and insurance and allied legislation may not be necessary whereby those with investment capital will be obligated, in certain years to be designated by the minister, to devote a fixed proportion to housing. That may be the only way in which enough money for housing can be found at the 6 per cent interest rate.
I have also assured a number of organizations at home that I would present a plea to the minister on his estimates, and even though he may be leaving the department I feel I must make the plea at this time. It has to do with the many low-cost homes that have been built in the past year. It may not have reached the minister's ears but there are a growing number of complaints that the quality of the buildings is not what it should be. Part of the reason seems to lie in the growing development of prefabricated sections of houses and in the growing tendency on the part of fly-by-night operators building N.H.A. homes not to hire union workers but to make use of moonlight labour and people who will work on week ends. When the taxpayers' money is being invested in housing I hope that their long term interest will be protected by suitable regulations or amendments to the National Housing Act whereby the quality of construction will be of a desirable standard.
The minister has performed wonders within the past 12 to 18 months with respect to the number of housing units that have been built. I believe that even the minister would now

agree that perhaps the time has come to devote greater attention to the problem of slum clearance and the supplying of low rental housing. I know that a little headway has been made over the past years. However, for so many long years we did practically nothing in Canada with regard to slum clearance or the building of low rental housing units. I believe we have probably reached the time when a much larger share of the money being invested in housing should be directed toward slum clearance and the supplying of adequate low rental housing for those people who have no hope of ever owning a home of their own.
I think the minister also had something to do with another proposed project with respect to which I have not heard of much progress being made. It has to do with expenditures in connection with harbours and rivers in the lower mainland of British Columbia. For the past several years there has been a move afoot, a wise one I believe, toward the development of an enlarged public authority to deal with matters concerning the Fraser river. For some years the ex-mayor of New Westminster has called for the enlargement of the New Westminster harbour board. I do not think that is exactly what is wanted by the areas concerned or even by some people in New Westminster. I believe the minister has been partly responsible for helping the idea along that there should be what I like to think of as a river authority with representation from the interested organizations and municipalities all the way from Mission to the mouth of the river. I hope that can be expedited a little before the new minister is appointed. Heaven only knows from what area of Canada he may come and how much or how little he may know about the need for an over-all authority on the Fraser river. Before the minister leaves the department I should very much like to see him take a hand in the matter and get together with the Minister of Transport. I know he has all kinds of advisers from the lower mainland on his side of the house and I should like him to try to see whether some progress cannot be made in this regard.
Like those who have spoken before me I too wish the minister well in his new department. Some of those who spoke sounded as if they thought the minister was leaving Canada but I look forward to seeing him in Canada almost as much as he has been hitherto.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time will, as usual, be brief, but I should like to draw to the attention of the minister one or two projects that I think the Department of Public Works should take

into consideration in the very near future. The hon. member for York-Scarborough has expressed the opinion of this group with respect to the appointment of the minister to the Department of External Affairs. However, I must say that while I regret to see him leaving the Department of Public Works nevertheless I extend to him my most sincere and best wishes. I know he will do a good job in his new department and I think that the twinkle in his eye will be one of his greatest assets as Secretary of State for External Affairs.
One project that I feel the department should consider in the near future is the provision of a building for Canada's national war museum. I find it is one of the places most favoured by visitors to Ottawa and the present building is very inadequate from the point of view of providing suitable accommodation for the exhibits. I believe that consideration should be given to providing a new building. I understand there are quite a number of other exhibits that could be put on display and this would be quite an asset from the point of view of the visitors who come to the museum. As I have already said, it is a most interesting place, especially to young people. This is one project that I think should be considered.
The second involves a group rather than one project. In Ottawa today we still have a large number of the old wartime buildings constructed during the war. While I realize that the department is eliminating them as quickly as possible, nevertheless some of them are getting into a very poor state of repair and they do not do justice to the civil servants who have to perform their duties in some of these buildings.
I feel that is something we should consider very seriously at the present time. While Canada is importing such a quantity of manufactured goods from other countries and taking away jobs from people who are in industry, I think we should do everything in our power to speed up our national works projects.
I believe it was last year that the steps over on the east side of the building were replaced which meant a great improvement. I feel that consideration should soon be given to providing new steps in front of the building. In my opinion the present ones are barely in keeping with the dignity of the House of Commons of the dominion of Canada. I am not saying they are dangerous but they are not as good as they should be and I understand they have been there for a long time.
I recall that when the minister spoke on his estimates some days ago he mentioned 66968-9-2771
Supply-Public Works
that his department was much concerned about the building of small post offices throughout the country. I could easily ask for several in the various villages and towns in my riding but I am not going to be so vain as that. Nothing creates more pride on the part of people in a small town or village than a public building on which they can display a flag several times a year. These buildings are wanted by the people and are respected by them. They are a source of pride and satisfaction to the people in the community. I hope the minister will take all these things into consideration and build as many public buildings as possible.
A great deal has been said about what has been done in the building of homes under the National Housing Act and I shall not repeat what has been said. There is no question but that during the months in which employment has not been too good in Canada the building of houses has been of considerable assistance in providing jobs for the working force. While it may be true that the saturation point is being reached in some areas there are many places that require additional homes and I trust there will be no slow-down in providing money for the construction of these homes under the act.
This concludes my remarks at this time. I am particularly interested in the construction of the national war museum building and I trust the project will be undertaken as expeditiously as possible.

Mr. Chairman, on this happy day for the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), may I join with those who have spoken before me to wish him much success in the diplomatic career he is undertaking. That appointment did not surprise me. There had been so much speculation on the matter. In fact, some were saying that this one or that one would be chosen, but I was convinced, and I do not want to belittle the other ministers, that the superior intelligence of the present minister, his remarkable energy, his devotion to work, the smile that he has kept since he became a member of the cabinet, and his consumate skill to have his estimates passed without too much difficulty, were already the indication of a first class diplomat. I am happy to join with my colleagues to congratulate him and to wish him great success in his new career.
Mr. Chairman, I rise not to test the diplomatic skill of the new Secretary of State for External Affairs, but merely to submit for his consideration a few projects which are very important for our area. I tell him right now that I shall be very brief.

Supply-Public Works
A problem which has been with us for many years and still is, is the matter of the national capital. Every Canadian would like to regard the national capital as a model. It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who, many years ago, said that everyone hopes to see Canada's capital develop into a Washington of the north.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the national capital plan will be quite incomplete unless adequate bridges are built to connect both sides of the Ottawa river. That is a matter of particular concern to the Minister of Public Works, since it comes under his department's responsibility.
New bridges across the Ottawa river are absolutely necessary if we want the numerous tourists visiting the national capital to take advantage of their stay among us to see the enchanting sites of the Gatineau, in those marvelous mountains that the national capital commission has adorned with beautiful roads and magnificent parks. We must at least give them the means to cross over.
At the present time, it is almost impossible to cross from one side to the other, at certain hours of the day. Furthermore, there are on the Quebec side more than 6,000 federal civil servants who must cross over three or four times a day, at least, to get to and back from work. In view of this, it takes them an hour or an hour and a quarter to cross over, while it should take them only fifteen minutes.
Such a situation cannot last indefinitely. Moreover, several residents of the city of Ottawa are employed on the Hull side and also have to cross the river to go to their work. It is almost inhuman to ask those people to get up at 6 o'clock in the morning in order to be in time for work at 8 o'clock on the other side of the river. Such is the situation! As a matter of fact, the present bridge is a disgrace for a national capital we are intent to beautify.
